overview: The Anushteginid Khwarazmshahs rose from governors in Khwarazm, south of the Aral Sea, to rulers of a large empire across Central Asia and Iran. Their hereditary line ruled from 1097 to 1231. This imported record is misleading: its southern Afghanistan and Pakistan outline omits Khwarazm and most of the empire, while its 1279 endpoint extends decades beyond the dynasty.

periods.title: An expanding empire
periods.summary: Successors extended independent rule far beyond Khwarazm.

periods.title: Invasion and resistance
periods.summary: Mongol conquest displaced the dynasty; its last ruler died in 1231.

sections.title: An empire and its ruling family

items.text: Qutb al-Din Muhammad became governor of Khwarazm in 1097, and his descendants made the office hereditary. His son Atsiz repeatedly challenged Seljuk authority but also submitted when circumstances required it. Independence emerged through campaigns, negotiations and changing alliances. The family’s early position was quite different from the enormous empire later ruled by Muhammad II.

Tekesh defeated the last Great Seljuk sultan, Toghril III, in 1194 and extended Khwarazmian power into western Iran. Winning territory did not guarantee a welcome for his soldiers. Resistance and attacks on Khwarazmian troops after his death reveal how fragile distant control could be, even when a ruler’s title and victories looked impressive.

Terken Khatun, Tekesh’s wife and Muhammad II’s mother, was an important political figure. Her marriage helped connect the dynasty with northern steppe military allies. After her son became ruler in 1200, she retained a powerful following and influence over decisions. Royal family relationships could shape armies and government, as well as life inside the palace.

sections.title: A busy city, water and skilled hands

items.text: At medieval Dehistan, archaeologists have identified water-supply works, bathhouses, sewage infrastructure and brick-paved surfaces. These are useful traces of washing, moving water and keeping a busy settlement functioning. The official heritage report describes the medieval city broadly, so every drain cannot be assigned to one Khwarazmian ruler. Sewage remains alone do not establish modern flushing toilets.

Dehistan also had workshops making bricks, bronze vessels and lamps, glazed ceramics and glass. Caravanserai remains mark places connected with travelers and trade. A pot or lamp involved specialist labor before it reached a household. The archaeological picture includes the makers and merchants who kept city life going alongside the more visible rulers and monumental buildings.

The mosque associated with Muhammad II is one of Dehistan’s major Khwarazmian monuments. Its surviving portal and nearby minaret belong to a city whose important buildings accumulated over centuries. Another minaret dates to 1004 or 1005, before this dynasty. Looking at a ruined skyline therefore requires sorting buildings by age, rather than giving every tower to the same king.

At Kunya-Urgench, the mausoleum attributed to Tekesh has a conical roof rising above a tall, many-sided drum. Brick patterns and surviving turquoise tiles decorate it, while the entrance has small projecting forms often compared to stalactites. The ICOMOS evaluation gives its date cautiously as around 1195. Its striking shape depended on skilled brickworkers and careful construction.

Jorjani arrived in Khwarazm in 1110 and wrote a Persian medical encyclopedia for Qutb al-Din Muhammad. Its ten books organized topics from anatomy and hygiene to fevers, surgery, skin problems and medicines. A reader could turn to a particular area of the body or kind of illness. This was a substantial working arrangement of medical knowledge, including ideas inherited from Avicenna.

Children’s teeth had a place in Jorjani’s medical writing. He discussed baby teeth, their replacement and teething, as well as the structure of adult teeth. Oral hygiene and toothpicks also received attention. These passages reveal practical concerns familiar to families: growing teeth, sore mouths and keeping teeth clean, even though medieval explanations and treatments differed from those used today.

Jorjani explained that completing his medical encyclopedia was difficult while he was also treating patients and directing the court pharmacy. He wanted to travel, collect plants and consult experts about medicines, but lacked the time. He therefore limited part of his discussion to familiar substances. Even a royal author could have too much work and too little time.

Zamakhshari compiled an Arabic-Persian dictionary for the ruler Atsiz. It grouped material under nouns, verbs and other grammatical categories, and also arranged words by meaning and rhyme. One surviving manuscript includes explanations in Chorasmian instead of Persian. Such books helped readers navigate a multilingual learned world; they do not by themselves tell us how many ordinary children attended school.

sections.title: A written sample and lives beyond conquest

items.text: “ذخيره خوارزمشاهى” means “The Treasure of Khvarazm’Shah”, the title of Jorjani’s Persian medical encyclopedia. This is the National Library of Medicine catalogue’s typeset transcription, linked to manuscript P5, folio 1b, line 11. That surviving copy is seventeenth-century; the work itself was composed for the Khwarazmian court after 1110. The later manuscript preserves a much older book.

The Mongol army destroyed Urgench in 1221, but the city was rebuilt and remained important afterward. Much later monuments in today’s archaeological park belong to those subsequent centuries. A dynasty’s defeat was a political ending, not a single final date for every street or family. The ruined city preserves several different periods of destruction, rebuilding and eventual abandonment.

ending.text: Mongol invasion shattered the empire. Jalal al-Din continued fighting after victories and defeats, fled across the Indus in 1221 and later campaigned in Iran and neighboring regions. He never recovered Khwarazm and was killed near Mayyafariqin in August 1231 while escaping renewed Mongol pressure. His death ended the ruling line’s struggle for an empire, although displaced troops and the region’s communities continued their histories.
